questions: What exactly is meant by “main factor” – does it refer to any factor, a proper factor, or specifically a prime factor?
Should the function return the factor as an integer, or as some other type (e.g., string) or wrapped in a container?
If n has multiple prime factors of the same maximal value (e.g., n = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3), which one should be returned, or does it matter?
How should the function behave when n is a perfect power of a prime (e.g., n = 27 = 3³) – is the largest prime factor 3 or should the exponent be considered?
Must the implementation validate that n is not prime, and if n is prime, should it raise an error, return None, or handle it differently?
Are there any performance or algorithmic constraints (e.g., must run in O(√n) time, avoid recursion, or use only standard library functions)?
Should the function treat negative inputs or zero as invalid, and if so, what exception or return value is expected?
Is the function required to handle very large integers (beyond typical 64‑bit range) and, if so, are there any limits on memory or time usage?
answers: 'Main factor' means the largest prime factor of n -- i.e., the definition is identical to 'largest prime factor', not a looser notion of importance.
The function should return the factor as a plain integer.
